summary: On 2026-08-06 Zenity Labs disclosed an active malware campaign, which it helped disrupt, on skills.sh, an open registry of AI-agent skills that CSO Online says is maintained by Vercel. Using look-alike GitHub organisations, a single actor impersonated two projects: Paperclip, an AI-agent orchestration platform, and Browser Use, a browser-automation tool. The actor cloned the legitimate projects and listed their skills on skills.sh. The skills first appeared on 2026-07-05 as clean copies. The surrounding repository was trojanised on 2026-07-06. On 2026-07-11 the skill documents were weaponised with setup instructions telling AI agents to download and execute a remote payload, or to install from attacker-controlled sources instead of the real package. The malicious instructions sat in a secondary document that agents opened only when installation was needed, and the skills pointed agents to one another. The payload was a credential harvester targeting SSH keys, cloud, Git and package-manager credentials, Kubernetes and Docker configuration, project .env files and AI-tool configuration on developer workstations, CI runners and agent workspaces. Two companion trojanised PyPI packages were flagged within hours of publication. The skills trended on skills.sh throughout July. By 2026-08-02 the family's displayed install counter exceeded 1.7 million; Zenity stresses this counter is aggregated and not unique per user, and that the number of victims is unknown. Zenity reports that Vercel and Microsoft/GitHub removed the listings and repositories within 12 hours of its outreach. AI agents were the execution vector, not the operator.

actor: PromptArmor researchers (coordinated disclosure with Snowflake)
impact: Per PromptArmor: the Cortex Code CLI could be induced to run commands outside its sandbox with the victim's Snowflake credentials, enabling actions such as data exfiltration or dropping tables. Demonstrated in testing; fixed in version 1.0.25; no in-the-wild exploitation reported.
mitigations: Keep the CLI updated to 1.0.25 or later, limit the Snowflake role an agent uses to least privilege and prefer browser-based authentication, treat untrusted content as a prompt-injection vector, and review agent permission and sandbox settings.
name: Snowflake Cortex Code CLI could be driven out of its sandbox via indirect prompt injection

sources.title: Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware

summary: PromptArmor disclosed on 2026-03-16, in coordination with Snowflake, that the Snowflake Cortex Code CLI could be manipulated through indirect prompt injection into running commands without human approval and outside the CLI's sandbox, using the victim's active Snowflake credentials to perform harmful actions such as data exfiltration or dropping tables. PromptArmor reported the flaw on 2026-02-05; Snowflake validated it on 2026-02-12 and deployed a fix on 2026-02-28 in version 1.0.25, applied automatically on next launch. The result came from controlled testing, where the attack succeeded about half the time, with no in-the-wild exploitation or affected users reported.

actor: Storm-3168 (Microsoft's designation for the actor Sysdig calls JADEPUFFER; no attribution stated)
impact: Per Microsoft: most of the more than 100 targeted Azure Storage accounts were deleted, along with a Key Vault, Function App and App Service plan; deletions of Azure SQL databases and of Site Recovery and Backup protection locks were attempted and failed; more than 30 successful storage-account key-retrieval requests followed. No ransom note was observed and no exfiltration confirmed.
mitigations: Microsoft recommends enabling Defender for Cloud plans for critical Azure workloads (Resource Manager, Storage, Key Vault, App Service, Databases).

Keep service-principal credentials, storage keys and other secrets out of source code, configuration files, public repositories and issues; treat any publicly exposed credential as compromised even after the original post is edited or deleted, and revoke or rotate it immediately.

Apply least privilege to service principals and other workload identities, and protect backup and recovery resources with independent safeguards such as resource locks and storage-account deletion protection, which blocked some deletions in this incident.
name: Storm-3168 (JADEPUFFER) used compromised Azure service principals for rapid, automated cloud resource destruction

sources.title: Storm-3168: Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals
JADEPUFFER-Linked Attackers Used Compromised Service Principals to Delete Azure Resources

summary: On 2026-09-25 Microsoft Security Research reported destructive Azure activity by the actor Sysdig calls JADEPUFFER, which Microsoft tracks as Storm-3168, under the headline "Agentic-driven cloud attacks using compromised service principals". In early June 2026, in one victim tenant, two compromised service principals carried out the activity. One enumerated the Azure environment for about 15.5 hours. The other, after further discovery, ran a destructive sequence lasting about seven minutes. It made more than 100 storage-account deletion attempts, most of which succeeded, deleted a Key Vault, Function App and App Service plan, failed to delete several SQL databases and recovery-protection locks, and then retrieved storage-account access keys. Microsoft could not confirm how the identities were compromised, though one service principal's secret had earlier been exposed in a public GitHub issue by an employee of the affected organisation. It assesses the objective as ransomware-aligned but observed no ransom note and no confirmed exfiltration. Microsoft frames the activity as part of a shift toward AI-orchestrated attacks. Its stated evidence, however, is that the timing and division of work across identities and tokens "strongly indicates automated or scripted execution". No model, agent framework or AI artefact is cited.

actor: General Analysis researchers (proof-of-concept)
impact: Per General Analysis: an assistant on the Supabase MCP server could be induced via support-ticket content to read a private credentials table and write it into a customer-visible thread. Demonstrated on dummy data; no in-the-wild exploitation.
mitigations: General Analysis recommends scoping the MCP server to one project, using read-only access where writes aren't needed, keeping sensitive data out of reach, requiring manual review of tool calls and outputs that leave the workspace, treating retrieved content as data not instructions, and not relying on prompt-injection filters alone.
name: Supabase MCP server could be steered into exposing a private database table

sources.title: Supabase MCP can leak your entire SQL database

summary: General Analysis published on 2025-07-08 a demonstration that an AI assistant connected through the Supabase MCP server, running with a privileged database role, could be steered by instructions hidden in customer support-ticket content into reading a private table of integration credentials and writing them into a ticket thread visible to the customer. The test used a self-built project with dummy data and reports no in-the-wild exploitation; the article notes that even read-only access permits reads of data available to the database role. Supabase documents the prompt-injection pattern and offers configuration options; the post does not report a Supabase fix. It is catalogued as an agent-hijack prompt-injection product vulnerability.

actor: Unknown
impact: Per Sysdig: an internal PostgreSQL database dumped after entry through a Marimo notebook, with the full chain under an hour. No victim identified.
mitigations: Sysdig recommends prompt patching or disabling of vulnerable features, auditing and rotating credentials on exposed systems, visibility across all assets, retaining telemetry sufficient to investigate lateral movement, and runtime threat detection.
name: Attacker used an LLM agent to move from a Marimo notebook CVE to an internal database in under an hour

sources.title: AI agent at the wheel: How an attacker used LLMs to move from a CVE to an internal database in 4 pivots

summary: Sysdig reported on 2026-05-26 an intrusion it observed on 2026-05-10 in which an attacker compromised an internet-reachable Marimo notebook through CVE-2026-39987 and then moved through cloud and SSH access to an internal PostgreSQL database and dumped its contents, with the chain running end-to-end in under an hour. Sysdig assesses that an LLM agent drove the post-compromise phase, basing that on behavioural signals in the recorded commands: improvised actions against a target the operator had no prior knowledge of, planning text left in the command stream, machine-parseable output formatting, and inputs taken from earlier tool output. Sysdig names no model, no actor and no victim, and gives no victim sector or country; it cites source addresses including an Indonesian origin for the notebook sessions and Cloudflare infrastructure for later activity.

actor: Unknown (Hunt.io: low-to-medium confidence the operator is Chinese-speaking; no group named)

points.label: Thailand (Ministry of Finance, per Hunt.io)

impact: Per Hunt.io: several systems within the Ministry of Finance network compromised, including a web shell on a ministry web server, captured session material for an administrative panel and a document-management platform, and agent-driven enumeration of a directory holding personnel records. No evidence of exfiltration; the ministry has not confirmed a breach.
mitigations: Hunt.io recommends reviewing the HiveServer2 authentication mode (the default accepts any credentials) and enforcing its UDF blocklist.
Audit web roots for hidden PHP files named to imitate system caches, and alert on web server processes connecting to internal Hadoop service ports.
Patch sudo and polkit, disable WebDAV on remaining IIS 6.0 servers, and change default credentials on GlassFish admin consoles while restricting them to trusted networks.
Hunt.io notes exposed Hermes web panels and publicly browsable /hermes-results/ output directories can be found by banner and file-path searches.
name: Operator ran a Hermes agent unattended for post-compromise enumeration inside Thailand's Ministry of Finance network

sources.title: Thailand's Ministry of Finance Targeted With Hermes AI Agent Running Unattended, Hades Implant Staged
Hermes AI agent used to automate attack on Thai Finance Ministry

summary: Hunt.io, in research conducted jointly with researcher Bob Diachenko, reported on 2026-07-23 an intrusion targeting Thailand's Ministry of Finance that it says was largely driven by the open-source Hermes agent running in its unattended "YOLO" mode, which removes human approval prompts. Three open directories on a Hong Kong-hosted staging server, captured between 9 and 13 July 2026, held exploit code, web shells, tunnelling tools, scripts with hardcoded stolen credentials aimed at ministry mail and Hadoop infrastructure, a previously unreported Go implant the operator calls "Hades", and Hermes output logs. The logs show the agent, on the operator's instructions, running privilege-escalation and kernel-vulnerability assessments against a ministry host, enumerating services and binaries, and recursively searching a web directory of the Office of the Permanent Secretary that held personnel records dating back to 2012. Hunt.io says session material, a web shell deployed on a ministry web server and internal network access indicate several ministry systems were compromised, but it found no evidence the files were exfiltrated and could not determine how initial access was obtained; no recovered artifact shows Hades on a ministry machine. Most of the tooling was conventional and the exploited weaknesses (such as default Hadoop service credentials) are not AI-specific. The ministry has not publicly confirmed a breach. Hunt.io assesses with low-to-medium confidence that the operator is Chinese-speaking.

actor: Russian-speaking actor tracked by Trend Micro as bandcampro

points.label: Russia (Russian-speaking actor bandcampro, per Trend Micro)

impact: Per Trend Micro: a live command-and-control botnet built and operated with Gemini CLI controlling eight dental-clinic computers and accessing the clinic's practice database; related credential attacks and compromised merchant websites. No victim named.
mitigations: Trend Micro recommends prioritising behavioural detection over easily changed indicators, strengthening credential protections including phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication, and pairing takedowns with network-level blocking and monitoring for reconnection.
name: Russian-speaking operator used Google Gemini CLI to build and run a command-and-control botnet

sources.title: Six Minutes to Compromise: How 'Patriot Bait' Actor Used AI to Build and Deploy a C&C Botnet
Russian-Speaking Hacker Uses Google Gemini CLI to Control Botnet of Eight Dental Clinic PCs

summary: Trend Micro reported on 2026-07-14 that a Russian-speaking threat actor it tracks as "bandcampro" abused Google's Gemini CLI as the primary operational agent, consultant and interface to build, deploy and run a command-and-control botnet, with the operator supplying intent in natural language. Trend Micro states the AI handled server construction, deployment on a new virtual private server, infrastructure configuration, bot management and troubleshooting, and that it controlled eight computers at a dental clinic and accessed the clinic's practice database. Session logs cover 19 March to 21 April 2026. The actor's related activity included credential attacks, compromised merchant websites and planning of cryptocurrency fraud targeting elderly people in the US and Canada; the dental clinic's country and the victims are not named. The Hacker News corroborated the report.

actor: Unknown human attacker directing multiple AI agents (no nationality or group stated by Unit 42)
impact: Per Unit 42: internal networks, source-code repositories, a secrets-management system and CI/CD pipelines breached; root and administrative credentials and cloud access keys obtained; the victim's cloud AI endpoints used as attacker infrastructure. An infrastructure-as-code tampering attempt was blocked by branch protection. Operational timeline under ten hours.
mitigations: Unit 42 recommends treating AI models, API keys and AI integrations as core infrastructure with inventory, rate limits, least privilege and logging; preparing coordinated automated containment across identity, cloud and pipeline systems; monitoring for machine-speed behavioural patterns; and requiring multi-party review and immutable protections for infrastructure-as-code.
name: Unit 42 investigation: AI agents sped an enterprise intrusion and hijacked the victim's cloud AI infrastructure

sources.title: An AI-Assisted Cyber Attack: Inside a Unit 42 Investigation

summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported on 2026-09-02 an investigation into an intrusion in which a human attacker directed multiple frontier AI agents in parallel to compress the time between attack steps. The attacker breached internal networks, source-code repositories, a secrets-management system and CI/CD pipelines, obtained root and administrative credentials and cloud access keys, and used the victim's own cloud AI endpoints as post-compromise infrastructure, offloading compute cost to the victim. An attempt to tamper with infrastructure-as-code was blocked by branch-protection controls, and the attacker had an agent produce an audit-style report of the victim's security posture. Unit 42 states the operational timeline ran under ten hours, the attack did not depend on novel zero-days, and the human set objectives while specialized agents executed tasks, shared results and re-planned. Unit 42 updated the post to clarify the event was an intrusion, not ransomware; it names no victim, model or actor nationality, and bases the AI-agent assessment on observed parallel model calls and AI-generated scripts.

actor: Unnamed Chinese-speaking opportunistic exploit operator (no group named; Unit 42 states the actor is based in China)

points.label: China (actor location as stated by Unit 42)
Malaysia (government entity targeted, per Unit 42)

impact: Per Unit 42: no autonomous exploitation succeeded. Manual operations exfiltrated memory data from three Citrix NetScaler targets, achieved command execution on 11 Marimo notebook endpoints, and made reverse-shell attempts against nine Apache Tomcat servers and three IKE VPN endpoints, including sustained exploitation of a government entity in Malaysia. More than 460 targets were attempted in total.
mitigations: Unit 42 notes that target-side configuration (authentication on n8n form endpoints, and Langflow deployments without auto-login or public flows) stopped the autonomous exploitation attempts, and that targets with weaker defaults would have been susceptible.
Per Unit 42, OpenAI's provider-side safeguards refused policy-violating requests and its safety systems disabled an account believed to be linked to the campaign.
name: Operator ran a DeepSeek-powered Hermes Agent in autonomous exploitation attempts; confirmed impact came from manual exploitation

sources.title: Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks

sources.publisher: University of Texas Regional Security Operations Center
sources.title: An AI ran a cyberattack campaign on its own, and it picked its own targets

summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reported on 2026-07-30 a campaign by a Chinese-speaking opportunistic exploit operator who ran the open-source Hermes Agent framework, with DeepSeek as its reasoning engine and tasking over Telegram, as an autonomous offensive operator. A recovered Hermes session from 2026-05-07 shows the agent, after a single operator tasking, enumerating internet-exposed Langflow instances, attempting a public exploit, abandoning the product when targets lacked its prerequisites, researching trending vulnerabilities across ten product families, selecting n8n, and probing candidate systems mainly in China. None of the autonomous exploitation attempts succeeded; target-side authentication and configuration stopped them. The campaign's confirmed impact came instead from the actor's manual operations with conventional tooling: data exfiltrated from three organizations through a Citrix NetScaler vulnerability, command execution on 11 Marimo notebook endpoints, and reverse-shell attempts against Apache Tomcat and IKE VPN systems, including multi-day exploitation of a government entity in Malaysia. Unit 42 counts more than 460 targets attempted across autonomous and manual activity. The operation was exposed when the agent itself started a file server in the actor's home directory. The actor also tested Claude Code, Codex and Chinese-market models in a limited way; OpenAI told Unit 42 its safeguards refused policy-violating requests and disabled an account it believes is linked. Unit 42 states the actor is based in China. MITRE ATLAS catalogs the autonomous session as case study AML.CS0070. Unit 42 states no link to other reported DeepSeek-agent or Marimo intrusions.
